section.title: The Anointing and the Last Supper
section.sectionRationale: The passion begins. As the leaders plot and Judas bargains, a woman lavishes costly perfume on Jesus for His burial. At the Passover He unmasks His betrayer and institutes the Lord's Supper, declaring the bread His body and the cup His blood of the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins.
section.thesis: On the eve of the cross, extravagant devotion and cold betrayal stand side by side, while Jesus transforms the Passover into the memorial of His own death, giving His body and His covenant blood, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the plot to kill Jesus; the anointing at Bethany; Judas's bargain; the preparation of the Passover; and the Last Supper with the betrayer unmasked and the covenant meal instituted.

verses.text: When Jesus had finished saying all these things, He told His disciples,
“You know that the Passover is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”
At that time the chief priests and elders of the people assembled in the courtyard of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas,
and they conspired to arrest Jesus covertly and kill Him.
“But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.”
While Jesus was in Bethany in the home of Simon the Leper,
a woman came to Him with an alabaster jar of expensive {{myron|perfume}}, which she poured on His head as He reclined at the table.
When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and asked, “Why this waste?
This perfume could have been sold at a high price, and the money given to the poor.”
Aware of this, Jesus asked, “Why are you bothering this woman? She has done a beautiful deed to Me.
The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me.
By pouring this perfume on Me, she has prepared My body for burial.
Truly I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”
Then one of the Twelve, the one called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests
and asked, “What are you willing to give me if I hand Him over to you?” And they set out for him thirty pieces of silver.
So from then on Judas looked for an opportunity to betray Jesus.
On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the {{pascha|Passover}}?”
He answered, “Go into the city to a certain man and tell him that the Teacher says, ‘My time is near. I will keep the Passover with My disciples at your house.’”
So the disciples did as Jesus had directed them and prepared the Passover.

units.label: The Last Supper
units.note: this is My body, My blood of the covenant

verses.text: When evening came, Jesus was reclining with the twelve disciples.
And while they were eating, He said to them, “Truly I tell you, one of you will betray Me.”
They were deeply grieved and began to ask Him one after another, “Surely not I, Lord?”
Jesus answered, “The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me will betray Me.
The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed. It would be better for him if he had not been born.”
Then Judas, who would betray Him, said, “Surely not I, Rabbi?” Jesus answered, “You have said it yourself.”
While they were eating, Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “Take and eat; this is My body.”
Then He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you.
This is My blood of the {{diatheke|covenant}}, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
I tell you, I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father’s kingdom.”
And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

myron.gloss: Fragrant ointment or perfume, here very costly. The woman's lavish outpouring on Jesus' head is an act of anointing and, He says, a preparation of His body for burial, a beautiful deed that the gospel will forever remember.

pascha.gloss: Passover, the feast commemorating Israel's redemption from Egypt through the blood of the lamb. Jesus keeps this Passover and fills it with new meaning, for He is the true Lamb whose blood delivers His people from sin and death.

diatheke.gloss: Covenant, a binding arrangement God establishes. Jesus calls the cup His blood of the covenant, echoing Sinai and the new covenant of Jeremiah 31; His death seals the promise of forgiveness and a renewed relationship with God for many.

basic.context: Jesus tells His disciples that in two days, at Passover, He will be crucified. As the leaders plot His death, a woman anoints Him at Bethany with costly perfume; the disciples call it waste, but Jesus calls it a beautiful deed preparing Him for burial. Judas agrees to betray Him for thirty pieces of silver. At the Passover meal Jesus announces that one of them will betray Him, then takes bread and cup and gives new meaning to them: this is My body, this is My blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
basic.hermeneutics: Matthew frames the meal between devotion and betrayal, the woman and Judas, to show what draws near to Jesus and what turns away. The Supper transforms the Passover: Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, and His death establishes a new covenant. Read this is My body in the context of the covenant meal He is instituting, the memorial and means of grace for His church.
basic.originalLanguages: The woman pours out precious myron, perfume, for His burial. Jesus keeps the pascha, the Passover, and fills it with new meaning. And He calls the cup His blood of the diatheke, the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins.
basic.typology: The Passover lamb, whose blood spared Israel, is fulfilled in Christ, the Lamb of God. The covenant blood sprinkled at Sinai and the new covenant promised by Jeremiah are fulfilled in Jesus' blood of the covenant.
basic.christ: Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, willingly going to the cross as the Scriptures foretold. He is the covenant maker whose blood, poured out for many, secures the forgiveness of sins and looks ahead to the feast in the Father's kingdom.
basic.god: God's saving plan unfolds even through betrayal; the Son of Man goes as it is written. God establishes His covenant and grants forgiveness through the blood of His Son, and He will bring His people to the joy of His kingdom.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12 gives the Passover lamb. Exodus 24 gives the blood of the covenant at Sinai. Jeremiah 31 promises the new covenant with forgiveness of sins. Zechariah 11 lies behind the thirty pieces of silver.
basic.oneStory: The passion opens with a woman's costly love and a disciple's cold price on Jesus' head. At the Passover, Jesus reveals the meaning of the death now upon Him: He is the true Lamb, and His blood seals a new covenant of forgiveness for many. The exodus story finds its fulfillment as the greater deliverance begins, and the Supper He gives will carry His death to His people until He drinks with them anew in the kingdom.

context.literary:
Chapter 26 opens with the formula that has ended each of Matthew's great discourses, 'When Jesus had finished saying all these things,' and the word 'all' marks the last one. From here to the end of the Gospel Matthew tells one continuous story, and Jesus, who has been the teacher, becomes the one who is handed over. The very first sentence of the narrative says so: 'the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified,' verse 2.

Matthew tells these verses in a sandwich. The leaders plot in verses 3 to 5, the woman anoints Jesus in verses 6 to 13, and Judas goes to the chief priests in verses 14 to 16. The woman's act is set between two acts of treachery, so that a costly, unasked gift stands against a cold bargain. The leaders say 'not during the feast,' verse 5, and the story shows that their plan will be overruled, since the death will happen at the feast. The same structure continues into the meal, where the preparation, verses 17 to 19, the prediction of betrayal, verses 20 to 25, and the institution, verses 26 to 29, are held together by the word 'while they were eating,' verses 21 and 26.

Two pairs of questions frame the scene. The disciples ask about the Passover, 'Where do You want us to prepare?' verse 17, and then each asks 'Surely not I, Lord?' verse 22. Judas asks 'What are you willing to give me?' verse 15, and later 'Surely not I, Rabbi?' verse 25. Questions reveal hearts here as they did in the garden of Genesis 3.

Matthew compresses the meal. The words over the bread and the cup are very short and are set in the closest possible relation to the betrayal on one side and the hymn on the other. The passage ends not in a scene of grief but of singing, verse 30, which ties the cup to the fulfilment of the kingdom.
context.historical:
The Passover in Jesus' day was the high point of the Jewish year. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims, lambs were slain in the temple courts in the afternoon of the fourteenth of Nisan, and families ate the meal that night within the city. The feast commemorated the exodus: the lamb, the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs and the cups of wine all recalled the night when God passed over the houses marked with blood, Exodus 12:12-14. At that season the authorities feared unrest, which explains why the leaders decided to avoid the feast, verse 5. The meal was eaten reclining, a posture of freedom, which is why the Gospels say Jesus 'was reclining,' verse 20.

The host and guests would pass a dish, and the bread was dipped in a common bowl, so that 'the one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with Me' did not identify a single person but a table companion, verse 23. To betray a man with whom you have eaten broke the most basic bond of hospitality in the ancient world, and Psalm 41:9 had given the shape of that betrayal: 'my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.'

The anointing happened in Bethany, in the house of Simon the Leper, a man known by that name, presumably once healed of the disease. The jar was made of alabaster, a soft stone prized for holding costly oils, and 'expensive perfume' was worth a great deal; John says the equivalent of three hundred denarii, close to a labourer's year of wages, John 12:5. Anointing the head was a mark of honour at feasts, and anointing a body before burial was an act of love toward the dead. Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation due to a master for a gored slave, Exodus 21:32, so the price the priests set on Jesus was the price of a slave. Judas, who kept the group's money bag, John 12:6, took this price.

The meal ended with a hymn, and at Passover the Jewish tradition was to sing the Hallel, Psalms 113 to 118, so that Jesus and the Twelve probably went out singing the psalms of the exodus, including the one that begins 'Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good,' Psalm 118:1.
context.canonical:
This passage gathers more Old Testament threads than almost any other in the Gospels. The Passover itself is from Exodus 12. The blood of the covenant is the language of Exodus 24:8, when Moses sprinkled the people with blood and said 'This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you.' The new covenant is from Jeremiah 31:31-34, which promises a covenant not like the old one, written on the heart, in which the LORD says, 'I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.' The man who ate Jesus' bread and betrayed Him is the figure of Psalm 41:9. The thirty pieces of silver come from Zechariah 11:12-13, though Matthew 27:9-10 names Jeremiah, probably because he is joining Zechariah with Jeremiah's potter and field in chapters 18, 19 and 32. The poured out for 'many' reaches back to Isaiah 53:12, where the servant 'bore the sin of many,' and to Jesus' own saying in Matthew 20:28.

The institution is reported four times. Matthew and Mark give the words in nearly the same form; Luke adds 'new covenant' and 'do this in remembrance of Me,' Luke 22:19-20; Paul reports the same as something he 'received from the Lord' and handed on, 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, and adds that each time the church eats and drinks it 'proclaims the Lord's death until He comes.' Matthew is the only one who adds 'for the forgiveness of sins,' a phrase that echoes the angel's word at the beginning, 'He will save His people from their sins,' 1:21. John does not give the institution but gives the surrounding story of the foot washing and the bread dipped for Judas, John 13, and teaches the same truth in John 6:53-56.

The anointing is also told by Mark 14:3-9 and John 12:1-8, with a different detail of day and place, and Luke has a distinct event in a Pharisee's house, Luke 7:36-50. The act is taken up in Christian memory as promised, 'wherever this gospel is preached.' And Paul's words, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, show that the church read the whole passion as the fulfilment of the feast, as Peter does when he says we were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:18-19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wants his readers to see the cross before it happens as the decision of Jesus Himself. He opens the chapter with Jesus announcing the plot, not discovering it. The opponents say 'not during the feast,' and Jesus has already said the time is the Passover. The leaders think they set the date; Matthew shows that the Son of Man is the one who sets it, and that all that happens, including Judas' bargain, takes place 'just as it is written about Him,' verse 24.

He also wants readers to learn what true devotion looks like. The woman does not speak in Matthew's account, and the disciples, who speak a great deal, are rebuked. Her act is called 'a beautiful deed,' and Jesus gives it a meaning she may not have known: she has prepared Him for burial. Against this is Judas, who asks what he can get. Two ways of drawing near to Jesus stand side by side, and Matthew leaves no room for the idea that one can have both.

Then comes the Supper, in which Matthew explains how the death of Jesus is to be understood. It is not an accident nor merely a martyrdom. It is a covenant sacrifice, offered for many, which brings the forgiveness of sins and which a community is to remember. The last line, about drinking it anew in the Father's kingdom, tells the disciples that the death is not the end of the meal, since there will be a feast.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The anointing is recorded as an act that Jesus approves, but it is not a command that every believer must lavish money on worship. It was a singular act in preparation for His burial, and Jesus' remark that 'the poor you will always have with you' is not permission to neglect them. It echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, which says that because there will always be poor in the land, God's people are to 'open wide your hand.' The sentence is about the unrepeatable presence of Jesus at that moment, not a principle that charity can wait.

The words over the bread and the cup are an institution, and Luke and Paul record the command 'do this in remembrance of Me,' which Matthew does not repeat. The church's practice of the Lord's Supper rests on that command and on Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 11, and not on Matthew's narrative alone. The description of Judas' bargain and the disciples' failure is just that, a description, and it is not a pattern, though it is a warning about how close to Jesus a person can stand while still betraying Him.

debates.question: In what sense is the bread 'My body'?

views.label: The bread becomes the body in substance
views.case: The words are 'this is My body,' and Jesus Himself speaks them. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that when the words are spoken the bread is changed, so that what is received is truly Christ. They point to John 6:53-56, where Jesus says that His flesh is real food, and to Paul's statement that the bread is a sharing in the body of Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:16.

views.label: Christ is truly present with the bread, without a change of substance
views.case: Lutherans hold that the body and blood are really present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine. Reformed churches following Calvin teach a real spiritual presence, in which the Spirit lifts believers to feed on the living Christ in heaven.

views.label: The bread is a memorial and a sign
views.case: Others, in the line of Zwingli, hold that 'is' means 'represents,' as when Jesus says 'I am the door' or 'I am the vine,' and that the meal is a remembrance and a proclamation. They note that Jesus' body was in front of the disciples as He spoke.

debates.bearing: All the views agree that the meal is Jesus' own gift and that it is to be received with faith. They differ on how Christ is present, and the debate ought to be conducted in the light of the unity Paul wants the table to express, 1 Corinthians 10:17.

debates.question: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?

views.label: Yes, the Passover meal on the evening of Thursday
views.case: Matthew, Mark and Luke all say that the disciples prepared the Passover and that Jesus ate it with them, verses 17 to 19. The ritual details, reclining, the cups, the dipped dish and the hymn, fit a Passover meal.

views.label: It was a meal with Passover character but a day early
views.case: John speaks of the leaders not entering Pilate's headquarters so as not to be defiled and to eat the Passover, John 18:28, and calls the day of the crucifixion the preparation, John 19:14. Some conclude that Jesus held the meal before the official Passover, since He was to be the lamb at the hour of the sacrifice.

views.label: Different calendars or a wider use of 'Passover'
views.case: Some suggest that different groups kept the feast on different days, so that Jesus' meal and the temple's did not coincide. Others point out that 'Passover' could refer to the whole festival, including the meals eaten on the days after the lamb was slain.

debates.bearing: The matter is a puzzle of harmonisation. On every view the Gospels agree about what mattered: the meal took place within the Passover season, Jesus interpreted His death by it, and He died at the very time the Passover lambs were slain.

debates.question: Are the woman and the anointing the same as in John 12 and Luke 7?

views.label: Matthew, Mark and John report the same event
views.case: The place, Bethany, the cost of the perfume, the objection about the poor and Jesus' answer, 'the poor you will always have with you,' are all shared. John names the woman as Mary and sets it six days before the Passover, while Matthew and Mark place it after the temple discourses.

views.label: Luke's account is a separate event
views.case: Luke 7:36-50 is set in Galilee, the host is a Pharisee, the woman is a sinner who weeps, and the lesson is forgiveness. The shared detail of a woman, a jar and a host named Simon is real but the stories are different.

debates.bearing: Matthew leaves the woman unnamed, which keeps attention on the act, and the shared feature across the Gospels is that Jesus took her devotion as a sign of His burial.

study.originalLanguages:
The woman pours 'expensive perfume,' myron, from an alabaster jar, alabastron, verse 7. The word myron is used of fragrant ointments in contrast to plain olive oil, Matthew says she poured it on His head, and the verb for 'pour' is built on the same root as the one Jesus will use of His blood, 'poured out,' ekchynnomenon, in verse 28. The perfume poured out for His burial and the blood poured out for many are one movement. A further link is in the title: Christos means the Anointed One, from the verb chrio, and here a woman anoints the Anointed One just before His death.

Jesus calls her act 'a beautiful deed,' kalon ergon, verse 10, and the adjective kalos means fair or noble as well as good. The disciples' word for what she has done is apoleia, 'waste,' which is also the word used of loss and destruction. The word Jesus uses for what she did for His body, 'prepared it for burial,' is enetaphiasai, from entaphiazo, to get ready for entombment, a verb that appears in the New Testament only here and at Jesus' actual burial, John 19:40.

The word that runs through the chapter is paradidomi, 'hand over,' translated both 'be handed over,' verse 2, and 'betray,' verses 16, 21, 23, 24 and 25. Judas asks, 'What will you give me if I hand Him over?' verse 15. The same verb is used of the Servant in Isaiah 53 in the Greek Old Testament, where the Lord handed Him over for our sins, Isaiah 53:6 and 12. The verb that describes Judas' betrayal is the verb that describes the Father's gift, Romans 8:32. In the same sentence human malice and divine purpose are both at work, and Jesus says so in verse 24: He goes 'just as it is written,' and the man who betrays Him is still responsible.

At the table each disciple says 'Surely not I, Lord?' using kyrie, verse 22. Judas, when it is his turn, says 'Surely not I, Rabbi?' verse 25. In Matthew's Gospel Judas never calls Jesus Lord, only Rabbi. Jesus answers him, 'You have said it yourself,' sy eipas, a formula that neither denies nor wholly confirms but leaves the man with his own words.

Two different verbs introduce the blessings. Jesus 'spoke a blessing,' eulogesas, over the bread and 'gave thanks,' eucharistesas, over the cup, verses 26 and 27. The second verb gave the later church the word eucharist. The bread is addressed to all with two imperatives, 'take and eat,' labete phagete, and the cup with one that includes everyone, 'drink from it, all of you,' piete ex autou pantes.

Verse 28 is the center of the passage. 'This is My blood of the covenant,' to haima mou tes diathekes, repeats the Greek Old Testament of Exodus 24:8, 'the blood of the covenant,' with the possessive 'My' added. The word diatheke, covenant, is also the word for a will or testament. The blood is 'poured out for many,' peri pollon, and 'many' is commonly read as an open, inclusive word, as in Isaiah 53:12 and Matthew 20:28, where the Son of Man gives His life as a ransom for many. 'For the forgiveness of sins,' eis aphesin hamartion, is the phrase Mark and Luke use of John's baptism, Mark 1:4 and Luke 3:3. Only Matthew applies it to the cup, and it fulfils the angel's word at the start of the Gospel, 1:21.

In verse 29 Jesus will not drink 'the fruit of the vine' again 'until that day when I drink it anew,' kainon, with you in the Father's kingdom. Kainos means new in kind and not just in time. The hymn of verse 30, hymnesantes, is the verb form of 'hymn' and points to the traditional Hallel.

typology.fulfillment: In Egypt a lamb without defect was slain, its blood was placed on the doorframes, and God passed over every marked house, Exodus 12:13, 22-23. The meal was to be kept as a memorial. Jesus celebrates the feast and then speaks over the bread and cup words that point to Himself. Paul says directly, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and Peter speaks of the 'precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. The escalation is that the lamb's blood spared Israel's firstborn from one night's judgment, while Christ's blood delivers from sin and death for good. The type falls short because the Passover lamb was an animal taken by the family, while Jesus is the Lamb who gives Himself willingly.

typology.type: The blood of the covenant at Sinai, Exodus 24:6-8
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai Moses sprinkled half the blood on the altar and half on the people, and said, 'This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you.' The people had promised obedience, 'All that the LORD has spoken we will do,' Exodus 24:7. Jesus uses the same words, 'This is My blood of the covenant,' and so claims to be the sacrifice by which a covenant is sealed. The escalation is clear in Hebrews 9:19-22, which sets Moses' sprinkling with the blood of calves and goats beside Christ's own blood and says that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. The earlier covenant was ratified by a promise the people could not keep; the new one is sealed by a sacrifice that does the work for them.

typology.type: The new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah promised that the LORD would make 'a new covenant,' not like the one the fathers broke, in which His law would be written on hearts, all would know Him, and He would 'forgive their iniquities and remember their sins no more.' At the table Jesus says that this covenant is now established in His blood, and Luke and Paul make it explicit by adding 'new,' Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25. The correspondence is that forgiveness is the foundation of the new covenant, which is why Matthew adds 'for the forgiveness of sins.' The escalation is that the blood is the basis of the promise, and the Spirit applies it in the heart. The fulfilment is partial now and complete in the age to come, since the feast Jesus speaks of is still ahead.

typology.type: The anointing of the king and the preparation for burial
typology.fulfillment: In Israel prophets, priests and kings were anointed with oil, and the Messiah is the Anointed One. In the house of Simon, a woman pours oil on Jesus' head and unknowingly does what a prophet would do at a coronation. Jesus reads the same act as the preparation of His body for burial, and so the king's anointing and the dead man's anointing are joined in one gesture. The correspondence runs through the Gospel, since the same man is called King on the cross, 27:37, and laid in a tomb prepared with spices, John 19:39-40. This is an echo rather than a declared type, and the Gospels do not draw the link themselves, but the pairing of kingship and burial in a single act is exactly what the passion will carry out.

study.christ:
The passage reveals Christ first by showing who is in control. The leaders plan to arrest Him quietly and avoid the feast. Jesus, who knows the day, announces it in advance: 'the Passover is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified,' verse 2. Judas goes to bargain, but the Master has already named the time. Jesus tells His disciples where to prepare the room, and the household is ready, verses 17 to 19, because 'My time is near.' The word for time is kairos, an appointed moment. The cross is not an interruption of His mission but the appointed hour of it.

He is the one who receives worship. The woman pours perfume on Jesus' head, and Jesus defends her. He is not embarrassed by an act that treats Him as a king or even as more than a man. 'You will not always have Me,' verse 11, is the statement of someone who is the centre of the devotion of His people. At the same time the anointing is for burial. The Messiah is anointed for death, and He knows it.

At the table He appears as the host and the sacrifice at once. The head of a Passover meal spoke over the bread and the cup the traditional words about the exodus; Jesus speaks other words, 'this is My body,' 'this is My blood,' and He places Himself at the centre of the feast. The shed blood is the blood of the covenant, and the covenant is the new covenant of Jeremiah, in which sins are forgiven. The only person with authority to say 'for the forgiveness of sins' is God, and Jesus says it of His own death. Matthew has shown from the first chapter that He is the one who 'will save His people from their sins,' 1:21, and here we see how He does it.

He is the willing victim. Isaiah said of the servant that 'He poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12. Jesus speaks of His blood 'poured out for many,' and by saying 'The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him,' verse 24, shows that He has gone to the cross with the Scriptures in His hand. He is not pushed into it by Judas or Caiaphas. John records Jesus' own comment: 'No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord,' John 10:18.

He is also the faithful friend who treats the traitor with grace. Jesus does not expose Judas by name. He lets him take the bowl, answers his lie with 'You have said it yourself,' and lets him go. The same Lord who was grieved by the betrayal offers the bread to all the Twelve, and nothing in the account suggests that the invitation to Judas was different from that offered to the others.

And He looks beyond the table. 'I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father's kingdom,' verse 29. The Supper is not a farewell but a promise, since the Christ who is about to die expects to be at table again with His people, and the cross is the road to that feast.
study.god:
The passage shows a God whose purposes are not defeated by human sin but accomplished through it. The leaders plot, a disciple sells his Master, and the disciples run, and the Son of Man 'will go just as it is written about Him,' verse 24. Nothing in the account excuses Judas, for Jesus says 'woe to that man by whom He is betrayed,' and nothing suggests that Judas was a puppet. The Bible holds both truths in tension. Peter will later say in a single sentence that Jesus was 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge' and that wicked men nailed Him to a cross, Acts 2:23. God is not the author of evil, and yet He uses it for good, as Joseph told his brothers, 'You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good,' Genesis 50:20.

He is the God who keeps covenant. The Last Supper is the moment when the long line of covenants reaches its goal, from the promise to Abraham to the blood sprinkled at Sinai to Jeremiah's promise of a covenant of the heart. God does not abandon His people after they break the old covenant, because He establishes a new one at the cost of His own Son. The faithfulness of God is shown not in leaving the covenant unchanged but in fulfilling it at His own expense.

He is the God who forgives, and the forgiveness is costly. 'Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness,' Hebrews 9:22. The God who is holy does not pretend that sin is small, and the God who is merciful provides the sacrifice Himself. Leviticus 17:11 says that He gave the blood on the altar to make atonement, and here He gives the blood of His own Son. The passage keeps justice and mercy together by locating them in the same act.

He is the God who gives Himself. The Passover had been a feast of deliverance given by God to His people. Now the Son gives His own body and blood as the food and drink of the covenant community. The God who was once distant at Sinai, to be approached only through blood and mediators, now sits at table with His people, and says 'Take and eat.'

He is a God of joy. The meal ends with a hymn and a promise, and the language of the kingdom is the language of a feast. The cross is the cost; the table is the goal. For worship this means that the Lord's Supper is not mainly a sombre act but a thanksgiving, as the name eucharist says, in which the church remembers a death and anticipates a banquet.

Finally, He is a God who is not impressed by size. A woman's jar of perfume, a cup, a loaf: God's great acts are accomplished in a room, around a table, with ordinary things. The God who made heaven and earth receives a woman's gift and says it will be told wherever the gospel is preached, and He takes a loaf of bread and makes it the sign of His body. We may bring small things to Him, and He takes them seriously.

crossReferences.note: The Passover instruction explains what the disciples were preparing. God passes over the houses where blood is seen, and the day is to be a memorial for all generations. Jesus interprets His own death through this night, so that His blood becomes the blood by which judgment passes over His people.

Moses sealed the Sinai covenant by sprinkling blood and saying, 'This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you.' Jesus' words at the table, 'This is My blood of the covenant,' deliberately repeat the phrase and claim that His own blood is the seal of a covenant greater than Moses'.

The promise of a new covenant, with the law on the heart, a people who all know the LORD and sins forgiven and forgotten. Matthew's addition of 'for the forgiveness of sins' to the words over the cup shows that Jesus saw His death as the establishment of that covenant.

The prophet is paid thirty pieces of silver as a mockery of his work and throws them 'to the potter in the house of the LORD.' Matthew sees this pattern behind Judas' price, and in 27:3-10 the silver is thrown into the temple and used to buy the potter's field.

David's lament over a close friend who shared his bread and lifted his heel against him is the pattern of Jesus' own betrayal at the table. John quotes it directly in John 13:18. Jesus' words in verse 23 about the one who dipped his hand with Him recall it.

The Servant 'poured out His life unto death' and 'bore the sin of many.' Jesus' blood 'poured out for many' draws on both phrases. It shows that the death He describes at the table is the atoning death of the Suffering Servant, willingly accepted.

Luke's account of the Supper supplies what Matthew leaves out. It adds 'given for you' to the bread, 'do this in remembrance of Me,' and the word 'new' before covenant. Reading the two together gives the full institution and the command that the church has kept.

Paul's early report is the oldest written account of the Supper, 'on the night He was betrayed.' He adds that each time the church eats the bread and drinks the cup it 'proclaims the Lord's death until He comes,' which joins Matthew 26:29's promise of a future feast to the church's present practice.

John tells the anointing with the woman named as Mary, the perfume on Jesus' feet, and Judas as the one who complained, because he was a thief who took from the money bag. It confirms Jesus' reading of the act as preparation for burial and shows the motive behind the protest.

'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.' Paul states plainly what Matthew shows in the setting of the meal. The apostolic church understood the whole passion through the Passover, and Paul makes it the basis of a call to purity.

The writer retells the sprinkling of Sinai and concludes that 'without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.' It explains why the Supper speaks of blood and why the forgiveness Matthew names is bound to Jesus' death.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a good world and a promise made after the fall, that the woman's seed would crush the serpent. Everything since has been the story of how God would make good on that promise. The exodus was one of its great chapters: a people enslaved, a night of judgment, a lamb whose blood protected its household, and a morning of freedom. Israel kept the Passover every year because the saving story needed to be remembered. But the prophets also kept saying that the old arrangement was not enough, because the people broke the covenant, and a new one was needed.

This passage is where the two lines meet. Jesus keeps the Passover and in the same hour gives it a new centre. The feast that looked back to the exodus now looks forward to the cross, and what He gives His disciples is the covenant meal of the new exodus, in which the deliverance is not from Egypt but from sin and death. The old story is not discarded, but gathered up and completed. The lamb, the blood, the covenant and the meal all find their meaning in Him.

The passage also confronts the part of the story that is darkest. The fall of Genesis is repeated at the table: the disciple who sells his master, the leaders who plot, the friends who will leave. Human sin is not removed from the story at this point but is shown at its worst, and it is precisely within it that the saving act takes place. God's answer to the fall was never to ignore it but to bear it. The woman's costly gift stands for those who see what is happening and give themselves to Him.

After the passion, the meal continues in the life of the church. Wherever Christians break bread and take the cup they proclaim His death and look to His return. The Supper is a sign set between the cross and the kingdom, a reminder of what was done and a foretaste of what is coming. The promise of verse 29 anticipates it: Jesus will drink the cup again 'with you in My Father's kingdom.'

That kingdom is the new creation. Revelation shows the Lamb who was slain standing at the centre of the throne, Revelation 5:6, and pronounces a blessing on those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The covenant promise that God will be their God and they His people is fulfilled when God makes His dwelling with humanity, Revelation 21:3. The story that began with a garden and a broken fellowship ends with a feast and a restored one, and the table at which the disciples sat on the night of the betrayal is its pledge.

quiz.q: How did Jesus interpret the woman's anointing at Bethany?

options.text: As a beautiful deed that prepared His body for burial, to be remembered wherever the gospel is preached.
options.note: Verses 10-13 show Jesus honoring her act as burial preparation.

options.text: As a kind gesture that showed her love for Him.
options.note: It was loving, but Jesus gave it deeper meaning, preparation for His burial, which this omits.

options.text: As a wasteful act that should have benefited the poor.
options.note: That was the disciples' complaint, which Jesus rejected.

options.text: As an attempt to make Him a king.
options.note: Jesus tied it to His burial, not to political kingship.

quiz.q: What did Jesus say the cup represented at the Last Supper?

options.text: His blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
options.note: Verse 28 gives the covenant and forgiveness meaning of the cup.

options.text: A memorial of the exodus from Egypt.
options.note: The Passover recalls the exodus, but Jesus fills the cup with new meaning, His covenant blood, which this misses.

options.text: A symbol of the coming political kingdom.
options.note: He speaks of the Father's kingdom, but the cup's meaning is His blood poured out for forgiveness.

options.text: Simply an ordinary cup of wine with no meaning.
options.note: Jesus gives it profound covenantal significance.

quiz.q: How does Matthew present Jesus' death in this passage?

options.text: As the foretold, purposeful fulfillment of Scripture: the Son of Man goes as it is written.
options.note: Verses 2 and 24 present the cross as God's foretold plan, not mere tragedy.

options.text: As an unfortunate result of the leaders' plotting.
options.note: The plot is real, but Jesus foretells and embraces the cross as Scripture's fulfillment, which this reduces.

options.text: As something that took Jesus by surprise.
options.note: Jesus announces it in advance, showing no surprise.

options.text: As a defeat that ended His mission.
options.note: He presents it as the means of forgiveness and covenant, not defeat.

quiz.q: What is the significance of Judas's thirty pieces of silver?

options.text: It was the price of betrayal, echoing the rejected shepherd valued in Zechariah's prophecy.
options.note: The sum fulfills Zechariah 11:12-13, the price of a slave for the shepherd.

options.text: It was simply the payment Judas negotiated for his help.
options.note: It was a payment, but its prophetic weight as the price of betrayal is the deeper point.

options.text: It was a large fortune that made Judas wealthy.
options.note: Thirty pieces of silver was the price of a slave, not a great fortune.

options.text: It had no particular meaning in the story.
options.note: Matthew presents it as fulfilling Scripture, so it carries real significance.

questions: The woman gave something extravagant and was criticized for it. Where might wholehearted devotion to Jesus look like waste to others, and are you willing to offer it anyway?
Judas bargained Jesus away for silver. What smaller price are you sometimes tempted to accept in exchange for faithfulness to Christ?
At the table Jesus said the cup is His blood poured out for the forgiveness of your sins. How does dwelling on that change the way you come to the Lord's Supper?
Devotion and betrayal sat at the same table. When you examine your own heart, which way is it leaning toward Jesus right now?
Jesus looked past the cross to drinking anew in the Father's kingdom. How does the promise of that future feast strengthen you to follow Him through hard days?

translationNotes.note: On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread is literally on the first of the Unleavened; the meal Jesus prepares is the Passover, which He fills with new covenant meaning.
Some manuscripts read the new covenant; the blood of the covenant echoes Exodus 24:8, and poured out for many recalls the servant of Isaiah 53:12 who bore the sin of many.
The fruit of the vine and the promise to drink it anew in the Father's kingdom point beyond the cross to the messianic feast, the marriage supper of the Lamb.
